read.title: A 30-second introduction
read.text:
Hi, I'm Ahmed. I'm an operations manager at a concrete solutions company that works in Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

I run the Egypt office and support our teams in Riyadh and Dubai. My work covers pricing, operations, sales support and accounting, so I see the whole journey from the first quotation to the final invoice.

Right now, I'm focusing on using data and AI to make that journey faster and more accurate. For example, we're working on cutting the time it takes to prepare a quotation from days to hours.

read.title: What we do
read.text:
We're a specialist concrete services company. We help contractors cut, drill, scan, repair and strengthen concrete structures.

Our clients are mainly main contractors, developers and facility managers. A typical project is a building that needs new openings for pipes or ducts without damaging the structure.

What makes us different is speed and precision. We scan before we drill, so we avoid hitting rebar or cables, and we usually mobilize a team within forty-eight hours.

We're a specialist concrete services company. We cut, drill, scan and strengthen concrete for contractors and developers.
We've worked with other drilling companies before. What makes you different?
Two things. First, we always scan before we drill, so we don't hit rebar or cables. Second, we can usually mobilize within forty-eight hours.

Yes, we've completed over thirty projects there this year. I can send you a short reference list today.

read.title: The first two minutes
read.text:
The first two minutes of a call set the tone. Start with a short greeting and a light question, like "How's your week going?" Listen to the answer and respond briefly.

Don't stay in small talk for too long. After one or two exchanges, move to business with a clear transition: "Shall we get started?" Then state the purpose of the call and check the time: "Today I'd like to understand your project and see if we can help. We have about thirty minutes — does that still work for you?"

A clear opening shows respect for the client's time and makes you sound confident.

read.title: Safe topics, real connection
read.text:
Small talk is not about the weather. It's about showing that you see the other person. The safest topics in business are travel, work events, the city, and the other person's projects.

In the Gulf, people often talk about recent trips, big events like a trade show, or new projects in the city. Avoid politics, religion, salaries and personal problems.

A simple pattern works well: comment, question, share. For example: "I saw the new metro line is opening soon. Have you tried it yet? I used it last month in Riyadh, and it saved me an hour." Then listen, and keep it short.
read.ar: الـ Small talk هدفه توري إنك شايف الشخص. مواضيع آمنة: السفر، والمعارض، والمدينة، ومشاريعه. ابعد عن السياسة والدين والمرتبات والمشاكل الشخصية. الهيكل: تعليق، وسؤال، وتشارك حاجة عنك.

read.title: Listen more than you talk
read.text:
In a good client conversation, the client talks most of the time. Your job is to listen, show that you understood, and ask the next useful question.

Use three tools. First, short reactions: "I see", "Right", "That makes sense." Second, paraphrasing: "So, if I understand correctly, the main issue is the delay on site access." Third, follow-up questions that start with what, how or why: "What happens when the access is late?"

Avoid interrupting, and don't jump to your solution too early. A clear summary often builds more trust than a long explanation.

read.title: Never end a call without a next step
read.text:
Many good calls end with "Great, let's keep in touch" — and then nothing happens. A professional close has three parts: a short summary, a clear next step with an owner and a date, and a thank-you.

For example: "So, to sum up, you need openings for three floors, starting in March. On our side, I'll send a quotation by Thursday. Could you share the drawings by tomorrow? Thanks again for your time."

If the client isn't ready, agree on a follow-up date instead: "Shall I call you next Tuesday to see where things stand?"

read.title: When you can't hear clearly
read.text:
On calls, the biggest risk is not your grammar. It's misunderstanding a number, a date or a name. Never pretend you understood. It's completely normal to ask again.

Use polite, simple phrases: "Sorry, you broke up for a second. Could you repeat the last part?" or "Just to confirm, did you say fifteen or fifty?"

For numbers, read them back digit by digit: "So that's one-five, fifteen square meters." For names and emails, spell them using a simple alphabet: "A for Alpha, H for Hotel." A ten-second check can save a week of rework.

read.title: Is that your time or mine?
read.text:
When you work with Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, time zones and working days can cause confusion. Cairo is one hour behind Riyadh, and two hours behind Dubai most of the year. Weekends are also different from many European clients.

Always write the time zone: "Tuesday at 11:00 Dubai time (10:00 Riyadh)." Offer two options instead of asking "When are you free?" That makes it easy to say yes.

If you need to reschedule, apologize briefly, give a reason if helpful, and propose a new time in the same message.

read.title: Online meetings need clearer signals
read.text:
In video meetings, people can't read your body language easily, and there's often a short delay. So you need to signal more clearly.

When you share your screen, check first: "Can everyone see my screen?" Guide people: "On the left, you can see the timeline." To interrupt politely, use a short phrase and a reason: "Sorry to jump in — just a quick point on the dates." If two people speak at once, give way: "Go ahead, please."

When you finish your part, hand over clearly: "That's all from my side. Over to you, Sara."

read.title: The polite follow-up
read.text:
Most deals are not lost because of price. They are lost because nobody followed up. Clients are busy, and your quotation is one of many emails.

A good follow-up is short, friendly and useful. Instead of "Any update?", remind the client of the key point and add something small: an answer to a question, a new date, or a simple next step. For example: "Just following up on the quotation I sent last Tuesday. We still have a team available from the 15th. Would it help to have a quick call this week?"

Space your follow-ups: two or three days, then a week, then two weeks. After three follow-ups with no reply, send a polite closing message. It often gets the fastest answer.

read.title: Listen, own, fix, follow up
read.text:
When a client complains, the first goal is not to defend yourself. It's to make the client feel heard. Let them finish, then show you understood: "I understand — the team arrived two hours late, and your MEP crew was waiting."

Apologize for the impact, even before you know every detail: "I'm sorry for the disruption this caused." Avoid blaming others, like "the driver" or "traffic", in front of the client.

Then explain what you will do and when: "I'll check what happened and call you back by 3 p.m. with a clear plan." Finally, follow up as promised, and confirm what changes to prevent it from happening again. A complaint handled well often builds more trust than a project with no problems.

read.title: Putting it all together
read.text:
A strong client call has a simple shape. Open warmly and set the purpose. Introduce yourself and your company in thirty seconds. Ask questions and listen more than you talk. Confirm numbers and dates. Handle concerns calmly. Close with a summary and clear next steps.

You don't need perfect grammar to do this well. You need structure, a calm voice, and useful phrases you can say without thinking. That's why you've practiced each part separately.

Today, you'll put it all together in one recorded call. Listen back, use the checklist, and choose one thing to improve next time. Repeat the same call a week later and compare.
read.ar: المكالمة القوية ليها شكل بسيط: افتتاح وهدف، وتعريف في 30 ثانية، وأسئلة واستماع، وتأكيد الأرقام والتواريخ، والتعامل مع القلق بهدوء، وختام بملخص وخطوات. مش محتاج قواعد مثالية، محتاج هيكل وصوت هادي وعبارات جاهزة. سجّل، واسمع، واختار حاجة واحدة تحسّنها، وعيد بعد أسبوع.
